title: The Lost Ribbon
moral: True fairness means doing what is right, even when it may help someone else win.

pages.text:
Anaya's building was having a small sports evening.

There would be running races, lemon-and-spoon races, and a funny race where children had to walk with a book on their head.

"My head is not flat enough," said Rishi, trying once in the lobby. The book fell before he took two steps.

Anaya laughed. "Your head rejected the homework."

For the final race, each team had to wear a coloured ribbon. Anaya's team had a bright green ribbon tied around the wrist.

She liked it very much.

Just before the race, she saw Mehak standing near the gate. Mehak was new in the building and had not joined any team.

"Do you want to race?" Anaya asked.

Mehak shook her head. "No team."

Anaya looked at her own team. They already had enough runners.

Then she saw one boy from another team run past. His red ribbon slipped off and fell near the flowerpots.

Anaya picked it up.

No one had seen.

If she kept quiet, her team would have one less team to race against. They might win more easily.

The whistle blew for children to gather.

The red team was searching everywhere.

"Our ribbon is gone!" one child said.

Anaya held the ribbon tightly.

Then she looked at Mehak, still standing alone.

Winning felt exciting. But hiding the ribbon felt wrong.

Anaya walked to the red team.

"I found this near the flowers," she said.

Their captain smiled. "Thank you!"

Then Anaya turned to the organizer. "Can Mehak join their team? They need one more runner."

The race began. Children ran, shouted, and almost dropped their ribbons.

Rishi ran with so much seriousness that his shoe came half off, but he kept going like a brave soldier.

Everyone laughed and cheered.

In the end, Mehak's red team won. Anaya's team came second.

For a moment, Anaya felt a tiny pinch in her heart.

Then Mehak ran to her and held out the green winner's sticker she had received.

"You helped me race," Mehak said. "So this is partly yours."

Anaya smiled. The sticker was small. But that evening, it felt brighter than a trophy.
